title: Japanese Workers Tired of Unwritten Office Rules
paragraphs: Every workplace has its own rules. But in Japan, many workers say they are tired of the "unwritten rules" of office life, which are not official but which everyone is expected to follow.

A survey by Mfro, a media company based in Tokyo, asked 493 working adults which workplace manners they would most like to disappear. The respondents were men and women from their 20s to their 50s and older.

The rule that workers disliked most was strict email etiquette, chosen by 21.5% of people. In Japan, business emails often need to include long, polite greetings and fixed expressions, even for simple messages.

In second place, at 15.4%, was the custom of apologizing and bringing snacks for coworkers after taking a vacation. Many workers in Japan feel they should say sorry for causing trouble while they were away, even when they took holidays they were allowed to take.
Other unpopular rules included overly polite messages on work chat apps, chosen by 11%, too many greetings, at 9.1%, and having to share souvenirs from trips, at 4.7%.

The survey also asked how these rules affect workers. The most common answer was "mental fatigue," chosen by 35.3% of people. Others said the rules take up too much time, at 27.0%, or require extra effort, at 26.6%.

So why do people keep following these rules if they dislike them so much? About 36.1% said they were worried about what others would think, and 32.9% said the rules had simply become normal. Some people who had stopped following the rules said their coworkers looked at them strangely.

According to the article that reported the survey, these customs come more from peer pressure and tradition than from practical reasons. It suggested that remote work and younger generations may help the rules disappear over time.
